content.heading: A language for the work ahead.
content.body: A general-purpose programming language and toolchain built around one challenge: make useful software easier to write, understand, run, and deliver.
content.caption: Programming, re-examined
An editorial paraphrase of the project's own north-star question, not a quotation.

content.heading: Libraries and packages
content.body: Python has hundreds of thousands of packages and decades of libraries behind it. Guion ships 35 standard-library modules and a package manager that installs from a local path, a checksummed URL or the Guion package registry, whose log is signed and checked on install. The registry is live and holds two packages: frames, a data-frame library, and web, for web applications with sessions, protection against forged requests, checked templates and a router.
content.caption: Libraries and packages
content.note: The standard-library modules are listed in the language reference.

content.heading: Arrays and data science
content.body: NumPy and pandas make Python the default for numeric and data work. Guion now has native arrays and a first-party data-frame library, frames, but both are young. In the project's reports on one Apple M1 Pro, frames finishes five tested CSV workloads before pandas does from start to finish, mostly because pandas takes about 0.26 s to load. On compute alone, reading a large CSV is still about 3 times pandas, and array maths is about 1.4 to 2.3 times NumPy's.
content.caption: Arrays and data science
content.note: Earlier tests that reached NumPy through Python are retired and no longer cited. These figures are from the 11 and 12 November reports and have not been re-run on 0.5.0. The speed report is in the repository's evaluation results.

content.heading: A release you can use
content.body: Guion 0.7.0 is out for Linux (Debian 12 on ARM64 and x86_64), macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Windows (x86_64). It has a written stability policy, a live package registry, native arrays, closures, enums, generic functions, an editor server, and a web package with sessions, CSRF protection and checked templates. Both Mac builds are signed and notarized by Apple, so they open without a warning; the first launch checks with Apple and needs an internet connection. The Windows build is not signed, so Windows may warn the first time it runs, and the Intel Mac and Windows builds have had a build and a short smoke test, not the full test suite. Guion is still pre-1.0, and Python is a released language with a long track record.
content.caption: A release you can use
content.note: Each archive on the release page has a matching SHA-256 checksum file. On macOS and Linux, brew install rmichaelthomas/guion/guion and a one-line installer script also work.

content.heading: Learning it
content.body: In the project's comprehension study, assistants were given the shipped guides and five small tasks. Across 17 runs none took a wrong turn; four tasks closed in every run, and the fifth was reworded after early runs and then closed in its three reruns. That measures assistants, not people: whether a person can learn Guion from the guides and make a realistic change is not yet tested.
content.caption: Learning it
content.note: The receipts are in the repository under evaluation/comprehension/receipts. Learnability is still listed as an open outcome on the project status page.

content.heading: Beyond the tasks measured
content.body: Every number on this page is for a named program on a named machine against a named Python version. The server results come from one run on each of two cloud machines; an Intel Xeon server measured Guion slower on an earlier build, and GitHub's standard runners no longer offer one, so that result is unresolved. The Apple Silicon results were measured on early-November builds and have not been re-run on 0.5.0. Free-threaded Python and PyPy were not compared.
content.caption: Beyond the tasks measured
content.note: Overall competitiveness remains open, in the project's own words.
